articles.title: Plan for Japanese hub in Norwich announced by city council
articles.summary: A community group wants to give Japanese stories "a home in the heart of the city".
articles.body:
A community group is planning to breathe new life into a vacant former library by turning it into a cultural hub inspired by Japanese stories.

The not-for-profit Japan in Norwich group is working with the city council to take over the Old Library building.

Prof Simon Kaner, director of Japan in Norwich, has explained how the city's connections with the East Asian country go back more than 150 years.

He said the project would give these stories "a home in the heart of the city".

The Grade II listed building previously housed the Norfolk and Norwich Subscription Library from 1837 to 1976.

It was turned into a restaurant but has stood vacant since 2019.

Norwich City Council owns the building, but said Japan in Norwich - a community interest company - was its preferred partner.

Further work was needed on costs, timescales and funding sources, the council said.

As part of the vision, the library shelves could one day be filled with manga and graphic novels.

The space would be used for screenings, workshops and exhibitions.

Kaner, who is also executive director of the Sainsbury Institute for the Study of Japanese Arts and Cultures, pointed to the story of Norwich-born merchant Frederick Ringer.

He was a prominent businessman in Nagasaki, but returned home to spend his last days in Norwich, until his death in 1907. He was buried in the Rosary Cemetery near the railway station.

Pernille Rudlin, who has lived in the city for 20 years after moving from Japan, has also researched the city's links with the country.

She discovered some of the first Japanese people born in Norwich were believed to be descendants of Japanese performers who came to the city as part of acrobatic troupes in the 19th Century.

Speaking to Kayleigh Poacher on BBC Radio Norfolk, Rudlin said: "We would like this to be somewhere for anyone in Norwich that's got a story they want to develop and be inspired.

"There are so many creative people here. We are the city of stories."

Rudlin said that with "a young son myself" she knew that many of the thousands of students in Norwich "love" manga, anime culture and gaming.

"I know they really lack a third space, somewhere that isn't a pub or a nightclub where you can hang out and study and read."

Lucy Galvin, the Green Party council leader, said showcasing Norwich's long links with Japan would add an interesting dimension to the city's culture.

She said bringing the building "back into use as a place for reading, a place for stories in the city of stories; is a wonderful goal to have".

"Norwich is a unique city and to be able to have that extra offer and chance to upgrade the area just really makes it all stack up for us as a city council."

articles.title: BMW Australian PGA Championship: Cameron Smith in contention in his first DP World Tour event since LIV Golf collapse
articles.summary: Cameron Smith's eight-under second round has put him into contention; it is Australian's first event since LIV golf's demise; watch the BMW Australia PGA Championship throughout the week on Sky Sports Golf
articles.body:
Smith is playing in the Tour under a specific agreement, but made a slow start on day one of the BMW Australian PGA Championship with an opening round 71.

However, an eagle at the 14th by the 33-year-old in his second round helped him reach nine-under at the halfway mark to sit four off leader Nicolai von Dellingshausen ahead of the weekend.

Two birdies in the first three holes ensured Smith made a strong start and he got through his front nine at four-under.

A bogey at the 10th provided a setback, but the 2022 Open champion regrouped to get the shot back at the 11th before a superb approach helped Smith set up an eagle opportunity.

After he landed the eagle on the 14th, birdies on the 16th and 17th wrapped up a fine round of 64.

"It's only Friday, so we've still got a couple days to go, but it's nice to play the weekend," Smith said.

"It's nice to be in a position where I can compete and that's where I need to be to make my game better is competing and being under the pump a little bit. I kind of got in a bit of a groove and a bit of a rhythm today."

Northern Irishman Tom McKibbin is one shot ahead of Smith on 10-under after he hit 65 at The Lakes Golf Club on Friday.

Von Dellingshausen matched Smith with 64 to hold a three-shot lead on 13-under, but almost produced a hole-in-one at the 15th.

Later in the day, Robbie Minns did claim a hole-in-one with a seven iron at the 18th to win a BMW X5 40i.

Three players are tied for fourth on seven-under and England's Sam Bairstow is joint 18th on four-under after a second round score of 69.
